source_read: PDF (version of record), Curr Opin Psychiatry 27(4), pp. 269-275 = PDF pp. 1-7, every page rendered at 200 dpi and read column by column (abstract, Key Points, all sections, Figure 1, acknowledgements and the annotated reference list); every number checked on the rendered page. Step 1 written before the card was opened.

claims.overstatement: One sentence is one-sided. 'Several imaging studies and studies of self-control and decision-making found no difference in performance from comparison groups, although the review's conclusion states cognitive deficits as clear' leaves out that the same section reports large differences between people using several substances and controls on standard neuropsychological tests given outside the scanner (ref. 62), and an imaging study in which a brain metabolite tracked visuospatial and working-memory deficits (ref. 51) (p. 272). The review's evidence on cognition is mixed, not uniformly null; its 'clearly associated' (p. 272) and the conclusion (p. 273) still overstate it. Suggested: '...found no difference in performance from comparison groups, while one study found large differences on standard tests given outside the scanner; the review nevertheless calls the deficits clear'. Minor: (1) 'the DSM-IV diagnosis' - the review says the diagnosis was made historically under the DSM (pp. 269-270) without naming DSM-IV; the label is correct but the editors'. (2) 'in cross-sectional studies' is the editors' (accurate) description of refs 22, 23 and 31, which the review does not label. (3) 'Studies of self-control': the review cites one study of inhibitory control and one of decision-making.
claims.note: All numbers from this source re-found on the rendered pages: up to 75% of rave attenders using several substances, average five drugs at the last rave (p. 270; ref. 12 is a cluster analysis of underground rave attenders, p. 274); 18% lifetime limited-range use at 12-17 years and 34% before age 16 (p. 271; annotations 18.3% and 34.1%, p. 274); extended-range use 2% at 12-17 and 13.5% at 18-29 called panel survey designs (p. 271), whereas the annotations describe refs 22 and 23 as separate national samples of young adults and adolescents, ref. 22 with 13.2% (p. 274); sedative-and-alcohol class 1.3% last year (p. 271). Definitions (lifetime, 1-12 months, same occasion), the difficulty of measuring simultaneous use and its study mostly in smaller high-risk samples (p. 270), removal of polysubstance dependence from DSM-5 and population research recording only frequency (pp. 269-270), the three latent-class ranges (pp. 269-271) and the authors' judgment that prevention and treatment research is underdeveloped (pp. 269, 273) are all as the claim states. The review gives no search methods and does not appraise its sources (it covers work of roughly the previous 18 months, p. 270), and the Australian figures (refs 22, 23) come from the authors' own group, which supports the claim's 'second-hand' framing. The review also notes that in older groups people reporting polysubstance use in the past 12 months are very likely to report simultaneous use (ref. 22, p. 271).

anchors.locator: Abstract (Purpose of review; Recent findings; Summary)
anchors.extracted: Polysubstance use is common, particularly in some age groups and subcultures; recent latent-class models typically report a no-use or limited-range cluster (alcohol, tobacco, marijuana), a moderate-range cluster (adding amphetamine derivatives) and an extended-range cluster (adding non-medical prescription and other illicit drugs); prevalence varies with the population surveyed; wide-ranging use is linked with psychopathology, health problems and cognitive deficits; more prevalent among ravers and people already dependent; prevention and treatment research is underdeveloped.

Definition: more than one drug over a defined period, at the same time or at different times, therapeutic or recreational; in prevention and treatment usually several illicit drugs, sometimes licit or non-medical prescription drugs.

Polysubstance dependence was removed from DSM-5 (historically three or more substances excluding caffeine and nicotine, none dominating, dependence criteria met for the group); people are now diagnosed per substance on a severity continuum; most population research has recorded only frequency of use, not diagnostic criteria or severity. DSM-IV is not named.
The review covers key research published mainly in the previous 18 months, grouped by theme; no search method, criteria or appraisal described.

Polysubstance use is especially common in some subcultures such as ravers (dance club attendees): reports of up to 75% using several substances, with on average five drugs used at the last rave attended (ref. 12, a cluster analysis of underground rave attenders, p. 274).

anchors.locator: Prevalence and the Current Patterns of Multiple Substance Use, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: 2013 surveys in the USA, UK, Australia, Denmark and Latin America defined polysubstance use as lifetime use, use in the past 1-12 months, or simultaneous use on the same occasion; simultaneous use is hard to capture because asking about all drug pairs is impractical, and has mostly been assessed in smaller high-risk samples (club or bar patrons, clinical or subclinical groups).

Latent class analyses find a small number of clusters of increasing involvement: limited range (alcohol, tobacco, marijuana), moderate range (adding amphetamine derivatives), extended range (adding non-medical prescription and other illicit drugs) (refs 22-24, 31); Figure 1 is conceptual, prevalence not to scale.

Among teenagers use was mostly limited in range: 18% (lifetime, 12-17 years, ref. 23) to 34% (before age 16, ref. 18) report limited-range use; in older groups people reporting past-12-month polysubstance use are very likely to report simultaneous use (ref. 22).
An Australian nationally representative survey found a small cluster of young adults using sedatives and alcohol, last-year prevalence 1.3% (ref. 22).

The review says limited-range use in adolescence may raise the risk of expanded use in young adulthood and that panel survey designs show extended-range use of 2% at 12-17 years and 13.5% at 18-29 years (refs 22, 23); club and dance venues show widespread use, far above other venues (refs 25, 28).

anchors.locator: Reference list, annotations to refs 18, 22 and 23
anchors.extracted: Ref. 18: US nationally representative sample, 34.1% polydrug use before age 16. Ref. 22 (review authors' group): Australian national sample of young adults, polydrug use 13.2% (text says 13.5%), associated with men, low education and high income. Ref. 23 (review authors' group): Australian adolescents (National Drug Strategy Household Survey), 18.3% limited-range (lifetime) and 2% extended-range. Two different samples, not a panel.

Latent classes with wide-ranging use report more general psychological distress (refs 22, 23) and more anxiety and depression symptoms (ref. 31); drinkers with concurrent illicit use more generalized anxiety and major depression (ref. 40); in a treatment-seeking cannabis sample the wide-ranging class had more depression, anxiety, manic excitement and positive psychotic symptoms (ref. 41). Designs not stated by the review.

anchors.locator: Imaging and Neuropsychology Studies, 2nd paragraph (closing sentences)
anchors.extracted: The imaging studies just described, and recent studies of inhibitory control (ref. 57) and decision-making (ref. 58), found no difference in behavioural performance between people using several substances and controls, in contrast with the wider literature on impairment.

anchors.locator: Imaging and Neuropsychology Studies, 3rd paragraph; 1st paragraph (ref. 51)
anchors.extracted: Possible reasons for the null results: compensation, insensitive scanner tasks, low power. Large differences between people using several substances and controls were reported on standard tests of working memory, inhibition, flexibility, self-regulation and decision-making given outside the scanner (ref. 62); earlier in the section a metabolite level correlated with visuospatial and working-memory deficits (ref. 51). The review calls polysubstance use clearly associated with deficits but says specific relationships are hard to pin down because of differing methods, the wide range of substances used and low power.

anchors.locator: Prevention, Treatment, and Further Research, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Youth prevention shows modest, short-lived effects; prevention aimed at adults using several substances has pervasive methodological weaknesses; limited evidence on treating several problems at once versus one after another; future research should follow transitions in polysubstance use between ages 14 and 35 and measure frequency and severity.

The authors call it clear that people using several substances are at elevated risk of psychiatric and other conditions and have more pervasive cognitive deficits that raise the risk of poorer treatment outcomes (no study of treatment outcomes is cited); prevention and treatment approaches for polysubstance use are underdeveloped compared with single-substance treatment.

key_findings.correction: The review does not name DSM-IV: it says polysubstance dependence was diagnosed historically and refers to patients who 'previously met DSM Polysubstance Dependence criteria' (pp. 269-270). 'DSM-IV' is a correct gloss but should be marked as the editors', since the claim attributes it to the review. The rest (criteria, removal in DSM-5, severity continuum 2 to 11, population research recording frequency only) is confirmed.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist; two domains high, so overall high. Self-citation count (8 of 71) re-counted.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: certain and causal wording from cross-sectional associations; 'clear' cognitive deficits beside null behavioural findings; no evidence cited for poorer treatment outcomes.

missed: The review states that in older groups people reporting polysubstance use in the past 12 months are very likely to report simultaneous use (ref. 22, p. 271, Prevalence section, 3rd paragraph), i.e. one national survey did measure same-occasion use; relevant to the claim that simultaneous use is hard to capture in surveys.

The annotation to ref. 22 gives the correlates as men, low education and high income (p. 274), while the text cites refs 21 and 22 for being single, low education and being employed (p. 271): a second text-annotation mismatch for ref. 22 besides 13.5% vs 13.2%.

The claim's cognition sentence drops ref. 62 (large differences on standard tests outside the scanner), which the card's key finding 11 correctly includes; the editor should align the claim with the card.
